questions.question: What does it mean when `res.write(chunk)` returns `false`?
options: The chunk was rejected and must be sent again
The client has disconnected and the response is closed
Node is buffering data the consumer has not taken yet, so the producer should wait for the `drain` event
questions.explanation: A `false` return is the backpressure signal: the internal buffer is full. A well-behaved producer pauses and waits for `drain` before writing more.

questions.question: Why does the lesson prefer `pipeline()` from `node:stream/promises` over `.pipe()`?
options: `pipeline()` handles backpressure, forwards errors and destroys every stream in the chain if one fails, while `.pipe()` does not forward errors or clean up
`.pipe()` was removed from recent versions of Node
`.pipe()` only works with files, not HTTP responses
questions.explanation: `pipeline()` respects backpressure and, on failure, destroys all streams so file descriptors and database cursors are not leaked. `.pipe()` neither forwards errors nor cleans up.

questions.question: A user closes the tab halfway through a streamed CSV export. What happens with `await pipeline(...)` in Express 5?
options: The server keeps querying the database until the export finishes
Express automatically retries the response on a new connection
The source is destroyed and `pipeline` rejects with `ERR_STREAM_PREMATURE_CLOSE`, which should be filtered out of error logs
questions.explanation: When the socket closes, `pipeline` destroys the source (stopping the generator) and rejects with `ERR_STREAM_PREMATURE_CLOSE`. It is not a server bug, so catch it and return instead of logging a 500.

questions.question: Why does the SSE example write `: ping` every 25 seconds?
options: To tell `EventSource` which event ID to resume from
To keep the idle connection from being cut by load balancers, using an SSE comment line the browser ignores
To flush the compression middleware's buffer
To measure round-trip latency to the client
questions.explanation: Load balancers and proxies close idle connections. A periodic comment line (starting with `:`) keeps the connection alive without delivering an event to the browser.
